title: Bumping into things on the left: cranial nerve examination in a 78-year-old man admitted with suspected stroke
desc: This station involves a focused history and a cranial nerve examination of a 78-year-old man on the general medicine ward with a suspected stroke, who keeps bumping into things on his left. The candidate then interprets his formal visual fields, MRI brain, ECG and bloods, explains how visual field testing tells a posterior from a middle cerebral artery infarct, and plans stroke unit care, anticoagulation for newly found atrial fibrillation, secondary prevention and driving advice.
focus: Cranial nerve examination and localising a homonymous visual field defect to an arterial territory in posterior circulation stroke
diagnosis: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
stem: You are the intern on the General Medicine ward. Chris Kenneth, a 78-year-old retired man, was admitted last night with a suspected stroke. The nursing staff have noticed he has been having some trouble with his vision and have asked you to review him.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Kenneth and perform a cranial nerve examination (the vestibulocochlear nerve need not be tested), plus any other bedside examination relevant to a suspected stroke, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Mr Kenneth's formal visual field test, MRI brain report, ECG and blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Chris Kenneth, a 78-year-old retired electrician, admitted to the General Medicine ward last night with a suspected stroke. You are sitting in the chair beside your bed, alert, chatty and a little frustrated. You are sure the problem is your left eye. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Nurse's report (examiner: read this if the candidate asks the nurse what she has noticed): "This morning he knocked his water jug off the left side of his tray, didn't notice me when I came in on his left, and left the food on the left side of his plate, but he found it straight away when I told him to turn his head. Otherwise he's been fine overnight."

Opening line: "The nurses reckon something's wrong with my eyes. I think it's my left eye, doctor. I keep bumping into things on that side."

The vision (give only when asked):

  • Onset: you went to bed at about 10 pm the night before last feeling completely normal. You woke at 6.30 yesterday morning and it was already there.
  • What happened: you knocked your left shoulder on the bedroom doorframe and could not find your teacup on the left of the breakfast table. Margaret, your wife, made you come to hospital, and you got to ED at about 1 pm.
  • What it is like: things on your left "just aren't there" until you turn your head. It is not blurry, and it is not like a dark curtain. Reading is slow because you keep losing the start of each line.
  • Which eye: you assume it is the left eye. You have not tried covering each eye. If the candidate asks you to cover each eye in turn, you notice that the left side is missing in both eyes.
  • Course: no better and no worse since yesterday morning.
  • Eye symptoms: no eye pain or redness, no flashing lights or floaters, no double vision. No pain in the jaw when chewing and no tender scalp.

Other symptoms (give only when asked):

  • When you woke yesterday you had a dull ache at the back of your head (3 out of 10) and felt a bit unsteady getting out of bed. Both had gone by the afternoon. No room-spinning and no change in your hearing.
  • No weakness, numbness or tingling in your face, arms or legs. No trouble speaking, finding words or swallowing. Nobody has noticed your face drooping. No confusion.
  • Your sense of smell and taste are normal.
  • A previous episode (only if asked about earlier episodes): about 2 months ago, while you were watching TV, the left side of the screen went "fuzzy" for about 10 minutes and then came back. You put it down to being tired and told no one.
  • Heart (only if asked about palpitations or your heart): for about a year you have had the odd "flutter" in your chest. At a check-up last year your GP said your pulse was irregular and gave you a form for a heart monitor, but you never got round to it. No chest pain, breathlessness or blackouts.

Past medical history: high blood pressure for 15 years and high cholesterol. Cataract operations on both eyes 4 years ago, with good vision since. No diabetes, previous stroke, heart attack, bleeding problems or stomach ulcers.

Medicines: perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and paracetamol when needed. Since ED the nurses have given you "a little aspirin" (yesterday and this morning). You have never taken a blood thinner. No allergies. You wear reading glasses only.

Family history: your brother had a stroke at 80.

Social history: retired electrician. You live with Margaret (76) in a single-storey house. Margaret has macular degeneration and cannot drive, so you drive her to all her appointments, including her eye injections, and do the shopping. You are fully independent, walk the dog every day and have had no falls. Ex-smoker: 20 a day for 30 years, quit at 60. Two beers most nights.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: it is your left eye and you probably need new glasses.
  • Concern (say this when asked how it affects you, or about driving): "If I can't drive, who's going to get Margaret to her eye injections?"
  • Expectation: to go home in a day or two and see your optometrist.

Question to raise during the examination: "Is it my eye, doctor? Do I just need new glasses?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: alert, comfortable, not distressed. Average build (82 kg). No facial asymmetry. Pupils look equal, no ptosis. No rashes or scars on the face or scalp.
  • Observations (nurse's 08:00 set) and pulse: RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 158/86 mmHg, HR 88/min, irregularly irregular. Temperature 36.7 °C. Alert. Capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L. If the candidate listens: heart sounds dual, no murmur, no carotid bruits.
  • CN I: reports no change in smell.
  • CN II:
    • Visual acuity (Snellen, each eye, with his reading glasses off as he has no distance glasses): 6/9 right, 6/9 left.
    • Colour vision (Ishihara plates, if the candidate mentions them): all plates read correctly with each eye.
    • Visual fields by confrontation, each eye tested separately at about 1 m: right eye misses the target in both the upper and lower left (nasal) quadrants; left eye misses it in both the upper and lower left (temporal) quadrants. The right half of the field is normal in each eye. The defect stops at the vertical midline. Close to the centre, a red pin is still seen about 5 degrees to the left of fixation in each eye. If tested with both eyes open only: "he misses the target anywhere on the left".
    • Blind spot with a red pin: the right eye's blind spot is the same size as the examiner's. The left eye's blind spot lies within the missing left half-field and cannot be mapped.
    • Fundoscopy (if mentioned): clear media with lens implants. Optic discs pink with sharp margins, no swelling. Mild arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping. No haemorrhages, exudates or emboli.
  • CN III, IV, VI: pupils 3 mm, equal and round. Direct and consensual light reflexes normal in both eyes. Swinging light test: no relative afferent pupillary defect. Accommodation normal. Eye movements full in all directions (H pattern), smooth pursuit, no diplopia. No nystagmus.
  • CN V: pain (pinprick) and light touch normal and symmetrical in V1, V2 and V3. Masseters of normal bulk and contract equally on clenching. Jaw opens strongly against resistance without deviating, and moves normally from side to side. Jaw jerk present, not brisk. Corneal reflex (if mentioned): would be present on both sides.
  • CN VII: forehead wrinkles symmetrically. Eye closure strong against resistance. Cheeks hold air. Smile symmetrical. Pout normal. No facial weakness.
  • CN VIII: not required. If the candidate asks: hearing normal to conversation.
  • CN IX, X: voice normal, not hoarse. Palate rises symmetrically on saying "ah", uvula central. Cough strong. Gag reflex (if mentioned): would be present.
  • CN XI: shoulder shrug and head turning against resistance strong and equal.
  • CN XII: tongue of normal bulk, no fasciculations. Protrudes in the midline. Moves normally side to side.
  • If the candidate says they would complete the neurological examination: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical in all four limbs; plantars flexor; no pronator drift. Finger-nose and heel-shin normal. No tactile inattention (extinction) on simultaneous touch of both sides. Speech fluent, no dysarthria or dysphasia. He is aware of his visual problem. Gait steady.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms identity, explains the examination and gains consent. Exposes the face and shoulders and sits at eye level about 1 m from Mr Kenneth.
Explains each step in plain language, gives clear instructions, and acknowledges his frustration and concerns.
History
Characterises the visual problem:

kids.x: Onset and last known well: woke with it at 06:30 yesterday; normal at 22:00 the night before.

Nature and which eye: missing things on the left until he turns his head; asks whether one or both eyes are affected (he assumes the left eye and has not covered each eye); cataract surgery both eyes, reading glasses only.
Course and eye symptoms: unchanged since onset; no eye pain, flashes, floaters or double vision; trouble finding the start of each line when reading.

check.x: Screens for other stroke symptoms, including posterior circulation symptoms: weakness, numbness, facial droop, speech, swallowing, vertigo, imbalance, headache [only a mild occipital headache and unsteadiness on waking, both resolved].
Asks about previous transient episodes [10 minutes of fuzzy vision on the left 2 months ago].

Asks about vascular and cardiac risk factors: hypertension, high cholesterol, ex-smoker (30 pack-years), no diabetes; palpitations for a year and an irregular pulse found by the GP, never investigated.
Takes a medication, allergy and bleeding history: perindopril, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin since ED, never anticoagulated; no allergies; no bleeding problems or stomach ulcers.
Takes a social and functional history: lives with Margaret, who cannot drive; he drives her; independent; alcohol (two beers most nights).
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is his left eye and needs new glasses, worried about driving Margaret, expects to go home soon.
Examination
Asks for the observations and feels the radial pulse [BP 158/86, HR 88 irregularly irregular, glucose 6.4].
check.d: Award only if the irregular pulse is identified and named as possible atrial fibrillation.

check.x: General inspection: distress, habitus, facial or pupil asymmetry, rashes or scars [none].
CN I: asks about any change in smell [none].
CN II:

kids.x: Visual acuity with a Snellen chart, each eye separately, with distance correction or a pinhole [6/9 each eye].
Visual fields by confrontation, each eye separately, all four quadrants, at about 1 m [left homonymous hemianopia, central vision preserved].
kids.d: Award only if each eye is tested separately and the defect is described as homonymous.

kids.x: Mentions mapping the blind spot / tests central sparing with a red pin [right blind spot normal; left within the defect; central 5 degrees spared].
Mentions fundoscopy [no disc swelling, mild hypertensive changes].

check.x: CN III, IV, VI:

kids.x: Swinging light test for a relative afferent pupillary defect [none].
Eye movements in an H pattern, asking about diplopia and looking for nystagmus [full, no diplopia, no nystagmus].

check.x: CN V:

kids.x: Light touch in V1, V2 and V3 on both sides [normal].
Motor: clenches teeth while palpating the masseters, opens the jaw against resistance, moves the jaw side to side [normal].
Jaw jerk, and mentions the corneal reflex [normal].

check.x: CN VII: raises eyebrows, closes eyes tightly against resistance, puffs cheeks, smiles, pouts [no facial weakness].
CN IX, X: listens for hoarseness, watches palate and uvula on saying "ah", asks for a cough, mentions the gag reflex [normal].
CN XI: shoulder shrug and head turn against resistance [normal].
CN XII: tongue: inspects for wasting and fasciculations, then checks for deviation on protrusion [normal].
States they would complete the neurological examination: limb tone, power, reflexes and sensation, coordination, speech and inattention [all normal, no neglect].
Interpretation
Interprets the perimetry as a complete, congruous left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, localising the lesion behind the chiasm on the right, in the occipital cortex.
Interprets the MRI: acute infarct of the right medial occipital (calcarine) cortex in the PCA territory with right P2 occlusion; no haemorrhage, MCA territory normal, no extracranial stenosis.
Interprets the ECG as atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate and no ischaemia, newly identified, and the likely embolic source.
Interprets the bloods: normal renal function, FBC and coagulation allow a DOAC at full dose; normal glucose and TSH; LDL 3.0 on atorvastatin 40 mg, so the statin should be intensified.
Gives the most likely diagnosis as an acute ischaemic stroke in the right posterior cerebral artery territory (right occipital lobe), cardioembolic from AF, with supporting features.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: right MCA infarct, haemorrhage, occipital tumour and primary eye disease.
check.d: Award for at least three, each justified.

check.x: Explains how visual field testing separates a PCA from an MCA lesion (scored from the diagnosis question):

kids.x: A PCA (occipital) infarct often spares the macula because the macular cortex at the occipital pole also receives collaterals from the MCA.

An MCA lesion of the optic radiation usually splits the macula (macular sparing is characteristic of occipital cortex lesions), is often a quadrantanopia (inferior if parietal, superior if temporal), and usually comes with other MCA signs: face and arm weakness, sensory loss, neglect.

check.x: Management
States that he cannot have thrombolysis or clot retrieval (woke with symptoms, now beyond the treatment windows), and arranges stroke team review and transfer to stroke unit care.
Plans antithrombotic treatment for cardioembolic stroke:

kids.x: Continues aspirin until anticoagulated; the stroke team times the DOAC start by infarct size, early (within about 48 hours) for a minor to moderate stroke without haemorrhage.
Chooses a DOAC at the correct dose (apixaban 5 mg twice daily, no reduction criteria met) and stops aspirin once anticoagulated.

check.x: Plans other secondary prevention: statin intensified (atorvastatin 80 mg), long-term BP lowering, alcohol within guidelines, transthoracic echo.
Addresses ward safety and rehabilitation: falls precautions, approaching him and placing items on his right, orthoptist, OT for visual scanning and home assessment, physiotherapy.
Explains in plain language that this is a stroke in the vision area of the brain, not his eye, that glasses will not fix it, and that some recovery over months is possible but not certain.
Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words: new weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, trouble speaking or swallowing, worsening vision, sudden severe headache or drowsiness. In hospital, press the call bell at once; at home, call 000.
Explains bleeding warning signs once on the blood thinner: black stools, blood in urine, head strike after a fall.
check.d: Scored from the management answer or the fourth question.

check.x: Advises him not to drive (stroke: at least 4 weeks; hemianopia fails the Austroads field standard) and that he must notify the licensing authority.
Acknowledges the impact on Margaret and offers social work/transport help.
Mentions follow-up: stroke clinic and GP review.

part2.lead: It is later the same day. Mr Kenneth had an MRI brain this morning and formal visual field testing with the orthoptist this afternoon. Here are his visual field report, MRI report, ECG and blood results.
part2.patient:
• While the candidate explains the diagnosis or the management plan (question 2 or 3), ask: "So it's not my eye? Will glasses fix it? Will my sight come back?"
  • At question 4, after the examiner has put the question, ask: "Can I still drive? Margaret can't drive, and I take her to all her appointments." Be upset if told no, and settle if the candidate explains why kindly and offers help with transport.
  • Then ask: "What should I do if this happens again, or gets worse?"

handover.label: Formal visual fields (orthoptist, this afternoon)
handover.result:
Automated static perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 plus a 10-2 central field, SITA Standard), each eye tested separately with near correction, plus a binocular Esterman field.

Clinical details: 78-year-old man, suspected stroke, missing objects on the left since waking yesterday.

Reliability: fixation losses 1/14 (right) and 2/15 (left); false positives 3%, false negatives 4%. Reliable.

Right eye: dense loss of the entire left (nasal) hemifield, upper and lower, respecting the vertical meridian, with sparing of the central 5 degrees to the left of fixation. Right hemifield normal. Foveal threshold 34 dB.

Left eye: dense loss of the entire left (temporal) hemifield, upper and lower, respecting the vertical meridian, with sparing of the central 5 degrees to the left of fixation. Right hemifield normal. Foveal threshold 33 dB.

Comparison of the two eyes: the defects are the same shape and size in each eye (congruous).

Binocular Esterman field: all points left of the vertical meridian missed apart from those near fixation; horizontal extent about 95 degrees.

Conclusion: complete, congruous left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. The binocular field falls well short of the Austroads private vehicle visual field standard.
handover.model:
• Read: reliable test. Each eye loses the left half of the field, upper and lower, stopping at the vertical meridian: a complete left homonymous hemianopia. The defects match in the two eyes (congruous), and the central 5 degrees is spared (macular sparing). Normal foveal thresholds fit his preserved acuity.
  • For Mr Kenneth: a homonymous defect means a lesion behind the optic chiasm on the right, not an eye problem. A congruous defect with macular sparing localises it to the right occipital cortex, the territory of the right posterior cerebral artery. This confirms the confrontation findings.
  • What it changes: it points to a PCA rather than an MCA lesion. He does not meet the driving standard. He needs orthoptic and OT input for scanning strategies, and repeat fields later to document any recovery.

handover.label: MRI brain with MR angiography (this morning)
handover.result:
Examination: MRI brain (DWI, ADC, FLAIR, T2, SWI) with time-of-flight MR angiography of the intracranial and neck vessels. No gadolinium given.

Clinical details: 78-year-old man, woke yesterday with loss of vision on the left. Suspected stroke.

Comparison: non-contrast CT brain in ED yesterday at 13:40: subtle right occipital hypodensity, no haemorrhage.

Findings:

  • Diffusion: a 38 × 24 mm area of restricted diffusion (high DWI, low ADC signal) in the right medial occipital lobe, involving the cortex above and below the calcarine fissure (cuneus and lingual gyrus). The lateral tip of the right occipital pole is spared.
  • FLAIR and T2: mild corresponding hyperintensity, in keeping with an infarct about 1 to 2 days old. No mass effect.
  • SWI: no haemorrhage or haemorrhagic transformation.
  • Elsewhere: no other acute infarct. The right parietal and temporal lobes, including the optic radiations, are normal. Thalami, brainstem and cerebellum normal. Mild periventricular white matter change (Fazekas grade 1) and age-appropriate volume loss. No mass.
  • Intracranial MRA: abrupt loss of flow signal in the proximal P2 segment of the right posterior cerebral artery. Right P1 and both posterior communicating arteries patent. Basilar, vertebral, internal carotid, middle and anterior cerebral arteries normal.
  • Neck MRA: no significant stenosis of the carotid or vertebral arteries.

Conclusion: acute infarct in the right posterior cerebral artery territory (medial occipital lobe) with occlusion of the right P2 segment, appearances suggesting embolism. No haemorrhagic transformation. No middle cerebral artery territory infarct and no significant extracranial stenosis.
handover.model:
• Read: restricted diffusion along the right calcarine cortex, FLAIR change fitting 1 to 2 days, so an acute infarct. No blood on SWI. The MCA territory and optic radiations are normal. The right P2 is occluded, and the neck vessels show no stenosis.
  • For Mr Kenneth: this confirms an acute ischaemic stroke in the right PCA territory, matching the left homonymous hemianopia. The spared lateral occipital pole fits the macular sparing. An abrupt branch occlusion with clean neck vessels suggests embolism, in keeping with his AF. No haemorrhage or tumour.
  • What it changes: no bleeding, so antithrombotic treatment can continue. The infarct size (a PCA branch territory, without haemorrhagic transformation) guides when the stroke team starts anticoagulation. Carotid surgery is not relevant.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (today, 07:50)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, recorded at 07:50 today.

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 90/min.
  • Rhythm: irregularly irregular. No discernible P waves; fine fibrillatory baseline.
  • Axis: +30 degrees.
  • PR: not measurable.
  • QRS: 92 ms, normal morphology.
  • QTc: 432 ms.
  • ST and T: no ST elevation or depression; T waves normal.
  • Comparison: ED ECG yesterday at 13:30: the same rhythm, rate 96/min. GP ECG two years ago: sinus rhythm 70/min, otherwise normal.
handover.model:
• Read: atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate (about 90/min), normal axis, normal QRS and QTc, and no ischaemic changes. It was present yesterday too, and two years ago he was in sinus rhythm.
  • For Mr Kenneth: newly identified AF (probably present for a year, given his palpitations and the irregular pulse his GP found) is the likely source of the embolus to his right PCA. CHA2DS2-VA score 5 (age 75 or over 2, hypertension 1, stroke 2).
  • What it changes: he needs oral anticoagulation, not long-term antiplatelet therapy alone. The rate is controlled, so no rate control is needed now. A transthoracic echo assesses the heart. His TSH is normal.

handover.label: Bloods (today, 06:30)
handover.model:
• Read: FBC, electrolytes, creatinine 98 micromol/L (eGFR 63), liver tests and coagulation are all normal. Glucose 6.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.7% and TSH normal. LDL 3.0 mmol/L.
  • For Mr Kenneth: no metabolic mimic such as hypoglycaemia, no diabetes and no thyroid cause for the AF. Kidney function, platelets and clotting allow a DOAC. Apixaban needs no dose reduction: he has none of age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, or creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. His LDL is 3.0 mmol/L on atorvastatin 40 mg.
  • What it changes: apixaban 5 mg twice daily when the stroke team decides it is time to start. Increase the statin to atorvastatin 80 mg. These are the baselines for monitoring.

ask: You are now calling the stroke registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Chris Kenneth, including your interpretation of these results.

What is your most likely diagnosis, including the lobe and the artery involved, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer, including how the visual fields help you tell a PCA from an MCA infarct.
Outline your management of Mr Kenneth now, here on the general medicine ward.
Mr Kenneth asks whether he can drive and what he should do if this happens again or gets worse. Answer him.
expect:
• Identify: intern on General Medicine; Chris Kenneth, 78, admitted last night.
  • Situation: suspected stroke; nurses concerned about his vision. I found a left homonymous hemianopia and atrial fibrillation, also on the ED ECG.
  • Background: Last well 22:00, woke with it; probable TIA 2 months ago; HTN, lipids, ex-smoker; aspirin since ED.
  • Assessment: rest of the cranial nerves and limbs normal, no neglect. Perimetry: congruous left homonymous hemianopia, macula spared. MRI: acute right medial occipital infarct, right P2 occlusion, no haemorrhage. ECG: AF, rate 90. Creatinine 98, coagulation normal, LDL 3.0. Cardioembolic right PCA stroke.
  • Recommendation: stroke team review and stroke unit transfer today; DOAC timing; higher statin dose; orthoptics and OT.

Most likely: acute ischaemic stroke in the right posterior cerebral artery territory (right occipital lobe), cardioembolic from newly identified atrial fibrillation. For: woke with it; congruous, macula-sparing left homonymous hemianopia with no other deficit; DWI infarct along the right calcarine cortex with a P2 occlusion; AF on ECG; earlier transient episode.

  • Right MCA infarct of the optic radiation: against: no face or arm weakness, sensory loss or neglect; MCA territory normal on MRI. The fields separate them:
    • PCA (occipital cortex): complete, congruous hemianopia, often macula sparing, because the occipital pole also receives MCA collaterals; often an isolated defect.
    • MCA (optic radiation): macula usually split; often a quadrantanopia (inferior if parietal, superior if temporal), less congruous; usually with face and arm weakness, sensory loss, neglect.
  • Occipital haemorrhage: against: no blood on CT or SWI.
  • Eye disease: against: both eyes lose the left half-field up to the vertical midline; acuity 6/9, no RAPD, normal fundi.
  • Optional: occipital tumour: against: sudden onset, arterial-territory diffusion restriction, no mass effect.

1. Reperfusion: not eligible: woke with symptoms, now more than 24 hours, stable deficit.
  2. Stroke unit: stroke team review today and transfer to stroke unit care.
  3. Antithrombotic: continue aspirin for now. Start a DOAC for AF (CHA2DS2-VA 5): apixaban 5 mg twice daily (no dose reduction). The stroke team sets the start from infarct size, early (within about 48 hours) for a minor to moderate stroke without haemorrhage. Stop aspirin once anticoagulated.
  4. Secondary prevention: high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg); long-term BP lowering; alcohol within guidelines; transthoracic echo.
  5. Ward safety and rehabilitation: falls precautions, approach him and place things on his right; orthoptist, OT for visual scanning and home assessment, physio.
  6. Explain: a stroke in the vision area of the brain, not his eye; glasses will not fix it; some recovery is possible over months.

• Red flags, in plain words: new weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg; trouble speaking or swallowing; worsening vision; a sudden severe headache; drowsiness. On the ward, press the call bell at once; at home, call 000.
  • Bleeding: any bleeding, black stools, blood in the urine or a head strike after a fall once on the blood thinner: seek urgent review.
  • Driving: no driving for at least 4 weeks after a stroke, and his hemianopia does not meet the Austroads visual field standard, so he must not drive. He must tell the licensing authority. His eligibility can be reassessed by the licensing authority with repeat formal fields if his vision recovers. Acknowledges the impact on Margaret and offers social work help with transport.
  • Follow-up: stroke clinic after discharge and GP review.

ddx.dx: Right posterior cerebral artery territory ischaemic stroke (right medial occipital infarct), cardioembolic from atrial fibrillation
ddx.for: He woke with a congruous, macula-sparing left homonymous hemianopia and no other deficit; MRI shows an acute right calcarine infarct with a P2 occlusion; the ECG shows AF; and he had a transient left-sided visual episode 2 months ago.

ddx.dx: Right middle cerebral artery territory infarct involving the optic radiation
ddx.for: A right hemisphere stroke can produce a left homonymous hemianopia.
ddx.against: No face or arm weakness, sensory loss or neglect; the macula is spared; and the MRI shows the MCA territory and optic radiations are normal.

ddx.dx: Intracerebral haemorrhage in the right occipital lobe
ddx.for: Sudden onset with an occipital headache in a hypertensive 78-year-old.
ddx.against: No haemorrhage on the ED CT or on MRI susceptibility imaging.

ddx.for: An occipital mass produces the same field defect, and he is a 30 pack-year ex-smoker.
ddx.against: The onset was sudden, on waking, and the MRI shows diffusion restriction in an arterial territory with an occluded P2 and no mass effect.

ddx.dx: Primary eye disease (for example retinal artery occlusion or glaucoma in the left eye)
ddx.for: He believes the problem is his left eye and has had cataract surgery.
ddx.against: Both eyes lose the left half-field up to the vertical midline, acuity is 6/9 in each eye, there is no RAPD and the fundi are normal.

guide:
In Part 1 the history should be brief (about 3 minutes), leaving most of the time for the cranial nerve examination. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The vestibulocochlear nerve does not need to be tested. Accept a brief, mentioned-only test for colour vision, fundoscopy, corneal and gag reflexes. The task asks for any other bedside examination relevant to a suspected stroke, so the observations and pulse (item 13) are fairly expected. If the candidate tests the visual fields with both eyes open only, give the binocular finding and do not award the confrontation item, which needs each eye tested separately. Mr Kenneth reveals the earlier transient episode and his palpitations only when asked directly.

In Part 2 hand over all four results together and ask the four questions in order. Score the PCA versus MCA explanation (item 31) from the diagnosis question. While the candidate explains the diagnosis or management, Mr Kenneth asks whether it is his eye and whether glasses will fix it; item 37 is earned from that explanation. Score the bleeding warning signs (item 40) from the management answer or the fourth question. The fourth question puts his driving and "what if it happens again" questions; score the safety-netting items (39 to 43) from that answer.

A high-performing candidate pins down when he was last known well, screens for posterior circulation and other stroke symptoms, finds the earlier transient episode and the uninvestigated palpitations, and feels the irregular pulse. They test the fields in each eye separately and describe a left homonymous hemianopia with central sparing. In Part 2 they localise the lesion to the right occipital lobe and PCA, link it to the AF, and explain macular sparing by the occipital pole's dual supply. They plan stroke unit care, a correctly dosed DOAC with the stroke team setting the start, a higher statin dose and rehabilitation, and tell him kindly but clearly not to drive.

A borderline candidate tests the fields binocularly, calls it "left eye vision loss", or misses the irregular pulse. They name the wrong hemisphere, cannot explain macular sparing, start or stop antithrombotics without considering the AF, or leave driving out.
explain:
Localising a visual field defect

  • One eye only: the eye or optic nerve, in front of the chiasm. A relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced acuity or colour vision often go with it.
  • Bitemporal hemianopia: the chiasm, for example a pituitary tumour.
  • Homonymous defect (the same side in both eyes): behind the chiasm, on the opposite side of the brain.
    • Optic tract lesions give an incongruous defect.
    • Temporal lobe lesions of Meyer's loop give a contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
    • Parietal lesions of the optic radiation give an inferior quadrantanopia.
    • Occipital cortex lesions give a congruous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

Behind the lateral geniculate body the pupillary pathway is not involved, so the pupils and swinging light test are normal and acuity is usually preserved. Patients with a homonymous hemianopia often blame the eye on the affected side, as Mr Kenneth does. Testing each eye separately shows the true pattern.

Why Mr Kenneth has a right PCA infarct

He woke with a complete, congruous left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and no other deficit. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial occipital lobe, including the calcarine (primary visual) cortex. The macular representation at the occipital pole also receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery, so a PCA infarct often spares central vision. An MCA lesion of the optic radiation (parietal or temporal lobe) usually splits the macula (macular sparing is characteristic of occipital cortex lesions). It more often causes a quadrantanopia, and usually comes with contralateral face and arm weakness, sensory loss and, in the right hemisphere, neglect and visual inattention. Mr Kenneth has none of these, he is aware of his deficit, and his MRI shows an acute right calcarine infarct with a P2 occlusion and a normal MCA territory. PCA strokes can also cause sensory symptoms (thalamic branches), memory disturbance, visual hallucinations and, in the dominant hemisphere, alexia without agraphia.

Differentials

A right MCA infarct is the main alternative cause of a left homonymous hemianopia. The absent MCA signs, the macular sparing and the MRI argue against it. Haemorrhage is excluded by CT and SWI. A tumour is unlikely with a sudden onset and diffusion restriction in an arterial territory. Primary eye disease cannot produce a defect in both eyes that respects the vertical midline.

Mechanism: atrial fibrillation

An abrupt branch occlusion with normal neck vessels suggests embolism. The ECG shows AF that was missed in the community, and the transient episode of fuzzy vision on the left 2 months ago was probably a TIA. His CHA2DS2-VA score is 5, so he needs oral anticoagulation, not antiplatelet therapy alone.

Management

  • Reperfusion: not possible. He woke with the deficit and presented beyond the treatment windows.
  • Stroke unit care: every patient with stroke should be managed in a stroke unit by a multidisciplinary team (Acute Stroke Clinical Care Standard).
  • Antithrombotic therapy: aspirin, given once CT has excluded haemorrhage, continues until anticoagulation starts.
    • A DOAC is preferred to warfarin for non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg twice daily is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only if two of the following apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more. He has none.
    • The start date depends on infarct size and the absence of haemorrhagic transformation. Recent trials and the Living Stroke Guidelines support an early start for minor to moderate strokes, which the stroke team decides.
    • Stop aspirin once he is anticoagulated.
  • Other secondary prevention: a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg); an LDL target below 1.8 mmol/L applies where there is atherosclerotic disease, and his overall vascular risk supports intensifying; long-term BP lowering once past the acute phase; alcohol within NHMRC guidelines; stay smoke-free; transthoracic echocardiogram.
  • Hemianopia: falls precautions, and approaching him and placing his things on his right. Orthoptics, and OT for visual scanning training and a home assessment. Repeat formal fields to document recovery, which mostly happens in the first months.

Driving and safety netting

Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive:

  • A private driver should not drive for at least 4 weeks after a stroke.
  • A homonymous hemianopia does not meet the visual field standard.
  • He must tell the driver licensing authority, and the advice should be documented.
  • His eligibility can be reassessed by the licensing authority with repeat formal fields if his vision recovers.
  • Transport for Margaret should be discussed early, with social work help.

New weakness, numbness, facial droop, speech or swallowing difficulty, worsening vision, sudden severe headache or drowsiness means calling for help at once: the call bell on the ward, 000 at home. Bleeding on the anticoagulant needs urgent review. Follow-up: stroke clinic after discharge, GP review in 1 to 2 weeks, and repeat orthoptic visual fields.

Examination technique

Test confrontation fields in each eye separately, in all four quadrants, at about 1 m with the examiner's opposite eye closed. Test acuity with distance correction, or a pinhole if the patient has none. A red pin near fixation tests for macular sparing and maps the blind spot. The blind spot lies in each eye's temporal field, so in a left hemianopia the left eye's blind spot falls within the defect. Formal perimetry confirms and quantifies what confrontation suggests.
points: Localise a field defect: one eye only is in front of the chiasm, bitemporal is the chiasm, and homonymous is behind the chiasm on the opposite side.
A congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing points to the occipital cortex and the PCA. The occipital pole has a dual PCA and MCA supply, so central vision is often spared.
MCA lesions of the optic radiation usually split the macula, often give a quadrantanopia (inferior if parietal, superior if temporal) and come with face and arm weakness, sensory loss or neglect.
Test the visual fields in each eye separately. Patients with a homonymous hemianopia often think the eye on that side is the problem, and their pupils and acuity are normal.

Look for atrial fibrillation in every ischaemic stroke. Cardioembolic stroke needs a DOAC at the correct dose, with the stroke team timing the start by infarct size, plus stroke unit care and a high-intensity statin.
A homonymous hemianopia does not meet the Austroads visual field standard for driving. Tell the patient not to drive and that they must notify the licensing authority.
